title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
abstract: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)

bite.hook: New quantum transpilation method cuts circuit costs by up to 24.7% and speeds up routing by over 250 times.
tldr: Researchers developed a scalable transpilation method to overcome restricted connectivity in distributed superconducting quantum computers.
They combined a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic called the quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach.
The method reduces routing costs by up to 51.9% compared to baselines and maintains practical runtimes on a 399-qubit IBM Flamingo chip.
bite.whyItMatters: Scaling up quantum computers requires linking multiple smaller processor chips together, but limited physical wiring between them creates massive computing bottlenecks. This routing breakthrough makes multi-chip quantum processors dramatically more efficient and practical.
bite.eli5: Imagine trying to pass notes in a massive classroom where students can only talk to their immediate neighbors. If a student in the front needs to talk to someone in the back, messages get lost or take forever. This new method is like giving everyone a smart GPS map so they can pass notes across the room instantly without traffic jams.
